speaker: ALEX
text: Welcome back. Today we're setting up VS Code as an accessible place to do GitHub work, especially the kind of Markdown, review, and contribution work that shows up throughout this course.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And VS Code can sound a little intimidating if you've only used GitHub in the browser. Is this a whole new world, or just another way into the same projects?

speaker: ALEX
text: A bit of both. VS Code is a free, extensible code editor from Microsoft, and extensible means you can add features through extensions. GitHub.com is excellent for reading issues, reviewing pull requests, and having discussions, while VS Code is where editing, checking files, using Copilot, and moving through a repository can feel more direct.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the browser is still important. We're not replacing it.

speaker: ALEX
text: Not at all. You're adding a stronger workspace for creating. VS Code gives you a file tree, a full text editor, a built-in terminal, source control tools, settings, keyboard shortcuts, extensions, and accessibility features that can announce problems while you're working.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That last part is big. Finding an error after you push is stressful. Hearing about it while you're still editing is much better.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. This is Day 2 foundation work. The assumption is that you already completed the Day 1 walkthrough in GitHub's browser interface, including the Learning Room repository that was created for you.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So today is less about making a big contribution and more about making sure the editor is usable, signed in, and ready.

speaker: ALEX
text: Before installing anything, you can try VS Code right in your browser with github.dev. Open a repository on GitHub.com, then press the period key. After a few seconds, the repository opens in a VS Code-style editor in that same browser tab.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That period key shortcut feels almost hidden. Where does it work?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use it from a repository code page, such as the main page of your Learning Room repository or a folder or file view in the repository. It won't work from an issue page, a pull request conversation, or a random GitHub settings page.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if the period key doesn't do anything?

speaker: ALEX
text: You can go directly by changing the address to github.dev and the same owner and repository path, or look for repository page options that open the web editor. The period key is just the fastest route when you're already in the right place.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What do I get in github.dev once it opens?

speaker: ALEX
text: You get the Explorer file tree, the editor, search, source control views, many keyboard commands, Markdown editing, and a familiar VS Code layout. It's great for quick edits, reading a project, and practicing navigation without installing desktop VS Code.

speaker: JAMIE
text: But it's not exactly the same as desktop VS Code, right?

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. github.dev doesn't have a full local terminal, it can't run every tool, and Copilot support may require desktop VS Code or a Codespace depending on what you're trying to use. Desktop VS Code is better when you need installed extensions, command-line tools, local files, or deeper Copilot workflows.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So github.dev is perfect for quick orientation, and desktop VS Code is better when the project needs more power.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. For this workshop, github.dev is a low-friction bridge. You can open the Learning Room repository, test the interface, enable accessibility support, and confirm the main surfaces before doing heavier work.

speaker: JAMIE
text: The first thing I would want to do is make sure my screen reader and the editor are cooperating. How do I turn on screen reader mode?

speaker: ALEX
text: On Windows with NVDA or JAWS, press Shift+Alt+F1. You should hear confirmation that screen reader accessibility mode is on. On Mac with VoiceOver, VS Code is often already optimized, but if navigation feels wrong, open the Command Palette with Cmd+Shift+P and run Toggle Screen Reader Accessibility Mode.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What should change after it's on?

speaker: ALEX
text: VS Code adjusts the editor so screen readers get better announcements, including cursor movement, line content, suggestions, errors, and navigation context. It may change how some editor features behave so text editing is more reliable with assistive technology.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Are there screen reader-specific habits worth knowing?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. NVDA and JAWS users may need focus mode or forms mode when editing text, and browse mode can get in the way inside the editor. VoiceOver users should pay attention to whether focus is moving through the editor, sidebar, and panels as expected, and use the screen reader mode toggle if things feel off.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And VS Code has an accessibility help dialog too, right?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Press Control+Shift+H to open accessibility help. It tells you useful commands for the current context, including navigation help and ways to reach accessible views. If you forget a keyboard path, that help dialog is a good place to recover.

speaker: JAMIE
text: I want the editor to be chatty enough to be useful, but not so chatty that I can't think.

speaker: ALEX
text: That's where settings matter. In Settings, search for editor.accessibilitySupport and set it to on if automatic detection doesn't work well for you. Also search for screen reader announcements or accessibility verbosity settings so you can tune what VS Code speaks.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Audio cues are part of that too?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Audio cues are short sounds that can signal things like errors, warnings, breakpoints, folded regions, or terminal command completion. They don't replace speech, but they can add quick confirmation without making you stop and inspect the screen.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the baseline is: turn on support, confirm announcements, and adjust speech and sounds until the editor gives useful feedback.

speaker: ALEX
text: Once accessibility support is stable, the next skill is knowing the main areas of the VS Code window.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Give me the landmarks.

speaker: ALEX
text: There are five big areas to recognize: the Activity Bar, the sidebar, the editor, the panel area, and the Status Bar. The Activity Bar is the vertical strip of major tools, the sidebar changes based on the tool you picked, the editor is where files open, the panel is where things like Terminal and Problems can appear, and the Status Bar runs along the bottom.

speaker: JAMIE
text: The Activity Bar is the place with Explorer, Search, Source Control, Run, and Extensions?

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Explorer shows the file tree. Search finds text across the project. Source Control shows Git changes. Extensions lets you install add-ons. Accounts is usually near the bottom, and it is where GitHub sign-in lives.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if I don't want to hunt through the interface?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use the Command Palette. Control+Shift+P on Windows or Linux, Cmd+Shift+P on Mac. It's the most important VS Code shortcut because you can type the action you want, like Toggle Word Wrap, Preferences, or Accessible Diff Viewer, and run it from the keyboard.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How do I move between the sidebar, editor, terminal, and panels without getting lost?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use the keyboard commands for the surface you want, then listen for the announcement. Control+Shift+E opens Explorer, Control+Shift+F opens Search, Control+Shift+G opens Source Control, and Control+Shift+X opens Extensions. Control+` opens the integrated terminal in desktop VS Code, and Escape often returns focus out of temporary popups.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What's the difference between opening a folder and opening a file?

speaker: ALEX
text: Opening a file gives you one document. Opening a folder gives VS Code the project context: the file tree, search across files, Git status, extensions that activate for the project, and settings that belong to that workspace. For repository work, opening the folder is usually the better choice.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And for a Markdown file, headings can become navigation points, yes?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Open README.md, then press Control+Shift+O, or Cmd+Shift+O on Mac, to open the outline or symbols view. For Markdown, it lists headings, which makes long files much easier to scan with a keyboard and screen reader.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Where does GitHub sign-in happen inside VS Code?

speaker: ALEX
text: The most direct place is the Accounts button near the bottom of the Activity Bar. Activate it, choose the GitHub sign-in option, and follow the browser prompt. You can also open the Command Palette and search for Accounts if the button is hard to find.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How do I know sign-in worked?

speaker: ALEX
text: Return to the Accounts control and listen for your GitHub username. VS Code may also show account-related items in the Status Bar or ask permission for GitHub features when you first use them.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Status Bar is one of those places I forget about. What's usually in it?

speaker: ALEX
text: From left to right, it can include Git branch information, sync state, problems counts, live share or account indicators, line and column, indentation, encoding, language mode, notifications, and sometimes Copilot status. You can tab or arrow through many Status Bar items, and your screen reader should announce what each one does.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Copilot status is part of this setup check too.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. In desktop VS Code, look for the Copilot indicator in the Status Bar, use the Command Palette to search for Copilot commands, or try a small suggestion in a scratch file. If you're in github.dev and Copilot doesn't appear, that may be expected; you may need desktop VS Code or a Codespace.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And the Menu Bar is still there for people who prefer menus.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. The Menu Bar includes File, Edit, Selection, View, Go, Run, Terminal, and Help. On Windows and Linux, Alt usually moves focus to the Menu Bar. On Mac, the system menu is at the top of the screen, and VoiceOver users can navigate it with standard macOS commands.

speaker: JAMIE
text: There are a lot of entry points, but the pattern is reassuring: use a direct shortcut when you know it, and use the Command Palette when you don't.

speaker: ALEX
text: Settings are where you make VS Code feel less generic and more like your workspace.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Which settings should accessibility learners check first?

speaker: ALEX
text: Open Settings from the Command Palette or the menu, then search for accessibility. Check editor.accessibilitySupport, screen reader announcement or verbosity options, audio cues, font size, word wrap, cursor style, and line numbers if they affect how you navigate. The Settings editor also supports filters like modified settings and extension settings, which helps when you need to find what changed.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What about carrying those settings to another computer?

speaker: ALEX
text: That's Settings Sync. When you enable it, VS Code can sync settings, keyboard shortcuts, snippets, user tasks, extensions, and interface state across machines. If two machines disagree, VS Code may ask you to resolve a conflict instead of silently overwriting your setup.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Profiles sound related, but not identical.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. A profile is a named set of settings, extensions, and UI state. You might create a workshop profile with the accessibility settings, extensions, and shortcuts you want for this course, then switch back to another profile for different work. Profiles can also be exported and shared, and they can work alongside Settings Sync.

speaker: JAMIE
text: If shortcuts conflict with my screen reader, can I change them?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Open the Keyboard Shortcuts editor from the Command Palette, search for the command, activate the edit control, press the new key combination, and save it. If VS Code detects a conflict, review it before accepting the new shortcut.

speaker: JAMIE
text: I know this chapter focuses on setup, but learners also hear about terminals, extensions, and diffs. Can we place those on the map?

speaker: ALEX
text: Definitely. The integrated terminal is a command line inside VS Code, usually opened with Control+` on Windows or Linux, and from the Terminal menu as well. In github.dev, terminal support is limited, so use desktop VS Code or a Codespace when you need real commands.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Extensions are add-ons, right?

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. Open the Extensions view with Control+Shift+X, search for an extension, read its details, and install it if it fits your workflow. Extensions can add language support, GitHub tools, linters, themes, accessibility helpers, and project-specific features.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What about reviewing changes accessibly?

speaker: ALEX
text: VS Code includes an Accessible Diff Viewer. Open the Command Palette, search for Accessible Diff Viewer, and run it when you're reviewing file changes. It presents differences in a way that is easier to move through with speech than a purely visual side-by-side comparison.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Where does Source Control fit?

speaker: ALEX
text: The Source Control view shows changed files, lets you inspect diffs, stage changes, write commit messages, and work with Git. The full contribution workflow comes later, but recognizing the Source Control icon now makes later Git work less surprising.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And Copilot Chat and agents are desktop-focused?

speaker: ALEX
text: For serious use, yes. Desktop VS Code gives you the richer Copilot Chat experience, and later chapters use agent files and the living catalog of Accessibility Agents as part of contribution planning and review. For this setup chapter, you just need to know whether Copilot is available in your current environment.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So we're not trying to master every tool today. We're making sure the doors open, the announcements make sense, and the important rooms are findable.

speaker: ALEX
text: The practice for this chapter is a quick accessibility baseline. Plan about 10 to 15 minutes, and use either github.dev or desktop VS Code.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Walk me through it like I'm doing it now.

speaker: ALEX
text: Open your Learning Room repository on GitHub.com. Press the period key to launch github.dev, or open the same repository folder in desktop VS Code. Turn on screen reader mode, open Explorer with Control+Shift+E, open README.md, use Control+Shift+O for the outline, open the Command Palette with Control+Shift+P, check Accounts, and check Copilot status in the Status Bar if your environment supports it.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And then the evidence goes back to GitHub.com, not inside VS Code?

speaker: ALEX
text: Correct. Return to the assigned setup or Day 2 readiness issue and post a completion comment. Record whether you opened github.dev, enabled screen reader mode, signed in to GitHub, checked Copilot status, opened a file in Explorer, opened the outline or symbols view, and opened the Command Palette.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if one of those answers is no?

speaker: ALEX
text: Say where you got stuck. If the period key did nothing, check that you were on a repository code page. If the Explorer is empty, wait a few seconds and open Explorer again. If screen reader mode didn't announce, use the Command Palette and search for Screen Reader.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if Accounts or Copilot are hard to find?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use the Command Palette as your fallback. Search for Accounts to manage sign-in, and search for Copilot to see available commands. If Copilot doesn't show in github.dev, try desktop VS Code or a Codespace, or note that it was not available in your environment.

speaker: JAMIE
text: This makes setup feel like contribution work, not busywork.

speaker: ALEX
text: It is contribution work. A stable, accessible editor reduces friction and helps you make cleaner changes. When you can open the tool, sign in, confirm accessibility support, move through files, use the Command Palette, and report what worked, you're ready for the VS Code-based chapters that follow.
